summary: Extends the PASSporT signed-token format so that a phone call that has been diverted from its original destination can carry that fact. This information helps verification services judge whether a diverted call's caller identity is legitimate, and fits into the STIR framework against caller ID spoofing.

eli5.summary: When a phone call is forwarded, this adds a signed note saying it was forwarded and from where, so the final phone can check the call is not a fake.

subtitle: A signed note on a forwarded phone call saying where it was diverted from, so call-identity checks do not mistake forwarding for fraud.

tldr.problem: A forwarded call arrives with a signed identity naming a different called number than the one it reached, which looks like a cut-and-paste attack and is hard for the recipient to confirm.
tldr.mechanism: The retargeting entity adds a new PASSporT of type div whose div claim holds the previous destination, signed by a credential with authority over that number. A div-o variant nests the original PASSporT inside an opt claim.
tldr.outcome: Verification services can chain the PASSporTs and confirm a legitimate retargeting took place. The RFC also updates RFC 8224 so SIP 3xx responses may carry Identity header fields.

today: RFC 8946 is a Standards Track document (Proposed Standard) and updates RFC 8224. It has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why Diverted Calls Need a Marker
sections.content:
A PASSporT is a token based on the JSON Web Token (JWT) that carries signed information about the people in a communication. The STIR framework uses it to sign the caller's identity, and it also signs the called number. That second signature guards against a cut-and-paste attack: if Alice calls Bob, Bob must not be able to reuse Alice's Identity header in a new INVITE to Carol.

The catch is call forwarding. A call may legitimately reach Carol although the signed destination names Bob. Carol cannot easily tell forwarding from fraud. The SIP History-Info and Diversion header fields record retargeting but give no cryptographic assurance, and they log minor URI changes that do not change the real target.

This RFC therefore adds an explicit, signed indication that the original called number no longer reflects where the call is going. It defines a div PASSporT type for SIP and a div-o type for out-of-band and other non-SIP uses.
sections.eli5: If a letter addressed to Bob ends up at Carol's house, Carol wants proof that Bob really sent it on. This adds that proof to phone calls.

sections.title: The div PASSporT and Claim
sections.content:
A retargeting entity may act as an authentication service and create a new PASSporT of type div, which MUST contain the new div claim naming a previous destination. A new PASSporT is needed only when the canonical form of the dest identifier changes. If it does not change, a div PASSporT MUST NOT be produced.

The header includes "ppt":"div" and an x5u pointing to the retargeting entity's credential, and the PASSporT must use full form, not compact form. In the claims, the old destination becomes div, the new target becomes dest, orig is copied unchanged, and iat SHOULD normally be retained. If the original dest held several identifiers, exactly one is chosen for div.

The signing credential must have authority over the identifier in the div claim, not over orig as in baseline STIR. A div PASSporT MUST NOT contain an opt element.
sections.eli5: The person who forwards the call writes a note: "this was meant for number A, now going to number B", and signs it with A's own signature.

sections.title: Authentication Service Behavior in SIP
sections.content:
An authentication service adds a div PASSporT only to a SIP request that already has at least one Identity header field, and it MUST NOT remove the original Identity header. The retargeting entity SHOULD validate the existing Identity values first, though in high-volume settings it may leave that to the terminating verification service. The new Identity header carries the parameter ppt="div".

The dest value usually comes from the new Request-URI. When a request holds several non-div PASSporTs that share the same orig and dest, only one div PASSporT SHOULD be generated. If they differ, one SHOULD be generated for each. On a second retargeting, a new div PASSporT is made for each earlier div whose dest matches the current target.
sections.eli5: Each forwarding stop adds its own signed note and keeps all the older ones, so the notes form a trail.

sections.title: Verification Service Behavior
sections.content:
A verification service collects every valid Identity header, separates div PASSporTs from others, and links each div to an earlier PASSporT whose dest equals its div value, building chains. If a complete chain cannot be built, div validation cannot finish, though ordinary PASSporTs may still be validated.

  1. Compare the outermost dest to the call target, normally the Request-URI.
  2. Validate the outermost signature and that its credential has authority over the div identifier.
  3. Check that orig in the innermost PASSporT equals orig in the outermost, and in every div in between. If it changed, the whole chain is invalid.
  4. Check date freshness of the outermost PASSporT. Checking the innermost iat is RECOMMENDED; for transferred calls a window on the order of three hours might suffice.
  5. Validate the signature on every PASSporT in the chain, and ignore a chain whose innermost PASSporT has an unsupported ppt.

What to do with the result is local policy and outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.eli5: The final phone follows the trail of notes from the newest back to the first, checking each signature and making sure the caller's name never changed.

sections.title: The div-o Type and the opt Claim
sections.content:
Where separate Identity headers are impossible, such as out-of-band STIR, the div-o type is used. It has the same claims as div plus a mandatory opt ("Original PASSporT") element, which holds the full-form PASSporT it was created from, in the encoded format of RFC 8225 Appendix A.

opt MUST contain a quoted full-form PASSporT and MUST NOT contain a compact one. The retargeting service creates one div-o per received PASSporT. Verifiers need no chain assembly because nesting happens through opt, but they perform the same checks: each nested PASSporT shares the orig of its parent, and its dest corresponds to the parent's div. How PASSporTs travel is left to the using protocol.
sections.eli5: Instead of sending the old note alongside the new one, the new note has the old note folded up inside it.

sections.title: Redirection with 3xx Responses
sections.content:
An intermediary can redirect with a 3xx response instead of retargeting. Baseline STIR works fine in that case, because the caller's new request gets a PASSporT matching the new target. But a caller that records the original target may want to show the final recipient that the redirection was genuine.

So STIR-aware redirecting intermediaries MAY return one or more PASSporTs in Identity header fields in the backwards direction, acting as authentication services for div. This is why the RFC updates RFC 8224, to permit Identity header fields in SIP 300-class responses. Using them is OPTIONAL for the receiver. Redirecting can also lower the amplification risk of larger retargeted requests.
sections.eli5: Instead of passing the call along, a helper can say "try this other number" and attach a signed note proving the helper really said so.

sections.title: Tracking with History-Info
sections.content: The div element may carry more than a destination. For deployments that also use History-Info, an hi element can hold the History-Info index value, such as 1.2.1, so a PASSporT can be matched to the right History-Info entry. The RFC also notes that future extensions might add the reason for retargeting, as the SIP Diversion header does.
sections.eli5: The note can also say which line of the call's diary it belongs to.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Tracking forwarding exposes routing policies and can reveal relationships between identifiers of the same user. Usually this information goes to the called party, not the caller. A forwarding service that acts as an anonymizing proxy may not be able to offer a secure chain of retargeting.

Creating a div PASSporT is at the discretion of the retargeting entity, so if an intermediate number must stay confidential, no PASSporT should be created for it. The cost is that downstream parties cannot correlate the call with the original PASSporT. Larger PASSporTs could be an amplification vector for SIP DDoS attacks, and using 3xx redirection mitigates that. The div type gives bulk callers no extra power, since it identifies who did the forwarding.
sections.eli5: Writing down who forwarded a call can reveal private habits, so a forwarder who wants to keep a stop secret can just not write the note.
